chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
title: Jam sessions in California: Charlie Christian and the Whitman Brothers
summary: He was refused a seat next to Charlie Christian; Joe Comfort's electric bass and Maxwell Davis's playing.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, going back to the --

Those were the days, man. It's no fun no more. There's a couple of guys that have got a studio in the village, they call themselves -- they have a jam session and they're making noise. Everybody's doing what they want to do.
Did you use to do a lot of that?
I used to go to sessions, yeah.
Yeah. Just right off, any particular session stand out in your mind?
Yeah, with Charlie Christian came with
HEMLOCK ERASABLE
I wanted to sit in in the Whitman Brothers, and Joe Comfort was there, (inaudible) Nat King Cole.
This is Minton's?
No, this is California.
Oh, right.
And they wouldn't let me sit in.
Why?

I was just getting started. But Joe Comfort had an electric bass, I remember that. He invented it, I think. (Inaudible), you can't sit with him. You can't sit with Charlie Christian. That's Charlie Christian up there.
Yeah.
Who do you think you are? He was probably right.
Did you ever get to sit in?
Not with Christian, no.
Yeah.
Well, that's how bad -- he came in way out in the , looking for someplace to play. That's how bad guys wanted to play.
Yeah.

There's a guy named -- I got to tell you this guy -- there's a guy named Maxwell Davis. He was ghost writing for Divenchy Tompkin. He was a big sound like Ben Wilson and Coleman Hawkins and everything. One of the greatest
players -- I doubt -- if he's living, he's still . I know he hasn't gone back.
And he used to be pretty active with these sessions?
He was in the Whitman Brothers band.
Yeah.
They hired him because he played so good. They couldn't afford him but they wanted him because he played so great.
Yeah.
He wrote, transposed, everything. They give him another part to play and he'd transpose it. Very rare for a black man. (Unintelligible) an education.
